steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computer vision paper that introduces a new setting, domain-aware continual zero-shot learning (recognizing unseen classes in unseen domains over time), motivated by wildlife images from camera traps. Cover the motivation, gaps in prior work, our method and benchmarks, and a contributions list.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- CV for natural sciences; species recognition as motivation
- Challenges of images in the wild (backgrounds, new domains, new species)
- Prior work: continual zero-shot learning vs domain generalization -> DACZSL
- Limitations of existing works and our fixes -> DIN
- Benchmarks, results, contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- CV for natural sciences
  - deep learning CV accelerates natural science research (cite)
  - est. 8.7 million species on the planet, many may go extinct before documented (cite)
  - efficient classifier -> process images from the wild, identify rare/unknown species
- Challenges in the wild (cite)
  - camera traps in various locations; animals visit specific spots -> model may use background instead of animal
  - migration, weather/light changes, natural disasters -> must recognize wildlife on new backgrounds
  - Fig. 1: Odocoileus virginianus by day (top) vs night (bottom)
  - recognize species evolved for new environments; avoid bias to known species in common environments (cite)
- Prior work -> setting
  - goal: continually recognize unseen classes in unseen domains
  - Continual Zero-Shot Learning: continual recognition of unseen categories, trained only on seen classes (cite); no design to encode domain info
  - Domain Generalization: knowledge from seen domains -> unseen target domains (cite)
  - unified setting: Domain Aware Continual Zero-Shot Learning (DACZSL)
- Limitations + fixes
  - text representations like Word2Vec pre-trained on Google Corpus (cite) not discriminative for very similar, rare classes (wild animals, Fig. 1)
    - inspired by CLIP (cite), ALIGN (cite): Transformer backbone (cite) for class-name text; visually aligned class-wise prompt learning
  - parameterized classifier on visual features biased to seen classes, esp. across new domains
    - attribute prototypical mapping network + contrastive learning on attribute space
  - domain info inadequately considered -> adversarial training for domain- and task-invariant features
  - together: Domain-Invariant CZSL Network (DIN)
- Benchmarks + contributions
  - DomainNet-CZSL and iWildCam-CZSL by splitting DomainNet and iWildCam
  - superior to all baselines; ablation studies
  - contributions: new DACZSL problem, first on transferability across both domain and class; DIN (text extractor + prompt learning, adversarial training); two benchmarks, DIN significantly better than state of the art

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Computer vision driven by deep learning has become a crucial tool for speeding up research in the natural sciences. For example, it is estimated that there are 8.7 million species on our planet, and many of them may become extinct even before humans document them. An efficient classification algorithm can help process the huge amount of images captured in the wild, and so help identify rare and unknown species.

But designing visual models for images captured in the wild is very challenging. For example, wildlife images are often taken by camera traps that are deployed in different locations. Some animals may often visit specific locations, which can make the model recognize an animal by the background of the scene and not by the animal itself. Also, different factors like animal migration, changes in weather and light conditions, and natural disasters mean the system has to be able to recognize wildlife against new backgrounds. In Fig. 1, the top row shows an image of an Odocoileus virginianus during the day, and the bottom row shows the same species at night. On top of that, models are expected to recognize species that have evolved to live in new environments, and not be biased towards known species in common environments.

To solve tasks like these, we want to develop a deep learning algorithm that can continually recognize unseen classes in unseen domains. Previous efforts have tackled parts of these challenges. Continual Zero-Shot Learning is about continuously recognizing unseen categories with a model that is trained only on seen classes. But these models do not have a specialized design to encode domain information. On the other side, Domain Generalization tries to apply the knowledge learned from seen domains to unseen target domains. So we take the domain information into account and propose a generalized and unified setting, Domain Aware Continual Zero-Shot Learning (DACZSL).

- Limitations + fixes
  - Word2Vec pre-trained on Google Corpus (cite) not discriminative for very similar, rare classes (Fig. 1)
    - inspired by CLIP (cite), ALIGN (cite): Transformer backbone (cite) for class names; visually aligned class-wise prompt learning
  - parameterized classifier biased to seen classes -> attribute prototypical mapping network + contrastive learning on attribute space
  - domain info -> adversarial training, domain- and task-invariant features
  - Domain-Invariant CZSL Network (DIN)
- Benchmarks + contributions
  - DomainNet-CZSL, iWildCam-CZSL (split DomainNet, iWildCam); beats all baselines; ablations
  - contributions: DACZSL problem; DIN; two benchmarks

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Computer vision driven by deep learning has become a crucial tool for speeding up research in the natural sciences. For example, it is estimated that there are 8.7 million species on our planet, and many of them may become extinct even before humans document them. An efficient classification algorithm can help process the huge amount of images captured in the wild, and so help identify rare and unknown species.

But designing visual models for images captured in the wild is very challenging. For example, wildlife images are often taken by camera traps that are deployed in different locations. Some animals may often visit specific locations, which can make the model recognize an animal by the background of the scene and not by the animal itself. Also, different factors like animal migration, changes in weather and light conditions, and natural disasters mean the system has to be able to recognize wildlife against new backgrounds. In Fig. 1, the top row shows an image of an Odocoileus virginianus during the day, and the bottom row shows the same species at night. On top of that, models are expected to recognize species that have evolved to live in new environments, and not be biased towards known species in common environments.

To solve tasks like these, we want to develop a deep learning algorithm that can continually recognize unseen classes in unseen domains. Previous efforts have tackled parts of these challenges. Continual Zero-Shot Learning is about continuously recognizing unseen categories with a model that is trained only on seen classes. But these models do not have a specialized design to encode domain information. On the other side, Domain Generalization tries to apply the knowledge learned from seen domains to unseen target domains. So we take the domain information into account and propose a generalized and unified setting, Domain Aware Continual Zero-Shot Learning (DACZSL).

In this paper, we look again at the existing works in the DACZSL framework and find several limitations. First, the text representation techniques they use, like the Word2Vec representation pre-trained from the Google Corpus, can't give enough discriminative guidance to recognize very similar and rare classes, such as the wild animals shown in Fig. 1. Inspired by large-scale vision-language models like CLIP and ALIGN, we use a Transformer backbone to extract the text representation of class names. To make the class prompts more visually grounded, we also do visually aligned class-wise prompt learning. Second, training a parameterized classifier over visual features makes recognition biased towards seen classes when there are unseen classes, especially across new domains. We deal with this by using an attribute prototypical mapping network and contrastive learning on the attribute space. Third, existing methods don't consider domain information enough. To fix this, we use adversarial training to learn domain- and task-invariant features, which helps transfer knowledge across domains. Putting these improvements together, we introduce our method, Domain-Invariant CZSL Network (DIN).

To model the setting and evaluate our method, we propose two benchmarks, DomainNet-CZSL and iWildCam-CZSL, made by splitting the DomainNet and iWildCam datasets. Our method gets better experimental results on these two benchmarks than all the baseline models. We also run ablation studies to see the impact of each methodological choice. Our contributions are:

- • We introduce Domain Aware Continual Zero-Shot Learning (DACZSL), a novel problem and a step towards the real-world challenge of continuously understanding unseen classes in unseen domains. Our work is the first to look at the transferability of knowledge in scenarios with both domain and class.

- • We develop a novel DACZSL method, DIN. DIN gives informative and visually grounded text representations with an improved text extractor and prompt learning, and it learns domain- and task-invariant visual features by adversarial training.

- • We propose two benchmarks, DomainNet-CZSL and iWildCam-CZSL, that continually reveal data from new classes and new domains. With extensive experiments, we show that DIN significantly improves performance compared with state-of-the-art methods.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning-driven computer vision has emerged as a crucial tool for accelerating research in the natural sciences [1,2]. For example, our planet is estimated to have 8.7 million species, many of which may become extinct even before being documented by humans [3]. An efficient classification algorithm can assist in processing the vast amount of images captured in the wild, thereby helping to identify rare and unknown species.

However, designing visual models for images captured in the wild presents significant challenges [4]. For example, wildlife images are often taken by camera traps deployed in various locations. Some animals may frequently visit specific locations, which can cause the model to recognize an animal by the background of the scene rather than by the animal itself. Moreover, factors such as animal migration, changes in weather and light conditions, and natural disasters require the system to recognize wildlife against new backgrounds. As shown in Fig. 1, the top row shows an image of an Odocoileus virginianus during the day, while the bottom row shows the same species at night. Additionally, models are expected to recognize species that have evolved to thrive in new environments, avoiding bias towards known species in common environments [1,5].

To solve such tasks, we seek to develop a deep learning algorithm capable of continually recognizing unseen classes in unseen domains. Prior efforts have partially tackled these challenges. Continual Zero-Shot Learning emphasizes the continuous recognition of unseen categories with a model trained exclusively on seen classes [6,7,8]. However, these models lack a specialized design to encode domain information. Conversely, Domain Generalization aims to apply the knowledge learned from seen domains to unseen target domains [9,10,11]. We therefore take domain information into consideration and propose a generalized and unified setting, Domain Aware Continual Zero-Shot Learning (DACZSL).

In this paper, we reexamine existing works within the DACZSL framework and identify several limitations. First, the text representation techniques they employ, such as the Word2Vec representation pre-trained on the Google Corpus [12], are limited in providing discriminative guidance to recognize very similar and rare classes, such as the wild animals depicted in Fig. 1. Inspired by large-scale vision-language models like CLIP [13] and ALIGN [14], we leverage a Transformer backbone [15] to extract text representations of class names, and to improve the visual grounding of the class prompts, we further perform visually aligned class-wise prompt learning. Second, training a parameterized classifier over visual features leads to recognition biased towards seen classes when facing unseen classes, particularly across new domains. We address this with an attribute prototypical mapping network and contrastive learning on the attribute space. Third, existing methods inadequately consider domain information. To overcome this, we adopt adversarial training to learn domain- and task-invariant features, facilitating knowledge transfer across domains. Integrating these enhancements, we introduce our method, Domain-Invariant CZSL Network (DIN).

To model the setting and evaluate our method, we propose two benchmarks, DomainNet-CZSL and iWildCam-CZSL, by splitting the DomainNet and iWildCam datasets, respectively. Our method achieves superior experimental results on these two benchmarks compared to all baseline models. Furthermore, we conduct ablation studies to assess the impact of each methodological choice. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

- • We introduce Domain Aware Continual Zero-Shot Learning (DACZSL), a novel problem and a step towards the real-world challenge of continuously understanding unseen classes within unseen domains. Our work is the first to investigate the transferability of knowledge in scenarios characterized by both domain and class.

- • We develop a novel DACZSL method, denoted as DIN. DIN introduces informative and visually grounded text representations through an improved text extractor and prompt learning, and learns domain- and task-invariant visual features by adversarial training.

- • We propose two benchmarks, DomainNet-CZSL and iWildCam-CZSL, that continually reveal data from new classes and new domains. Through extensive experimentation, we demonstrate that DIN significantly improves performance compared with state-of-the-art methods.
